content.text: Just looking into this and it appears that we are at the stage of replacing
's encoding of the human readable message with some sort of machine readable data structure.
But we could just change the structure of the message to something like this.

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Length: 139
Link: <data:text/plain;base64,U3RhdGU6IEZhaWxlZApEYXRhOiBbaHR0cDovL2V4YW1wbGUub3JnL2JvYiwgaHR0cDovL3B1cmwub3JnL2RjL2VsZW1lbnRzLzEuMS90aXRsZSwgIkJvYmJpZSJdCkNvbnN0cmFpbnQ6IFN1YmplY3Qgbm90IGluIHJlcG9zaXRvcnkgZG9tYWluCg==>; rel="http://www.w3.org/ns/ldp#constrainedBy"
Content-Type: text/plain
Server: Jetty(8.1.16.v20140903)

State: Failed
Data: [http://example.org/bob, http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/title, "Bobbie"]
Constraint: Subject not in repository domain
The only other implementation I have seen is to create a webpage for each constraint and provide that link in the header. I like this way as the message is more closely tied to the actual data.
But I am not as well versed in the LDP Spec as some so I'd love some feedback.
, Are you suggesting to leave the "link" header as-is, but add a more descriptive error message in the response body at:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-http-commons/src/main/java/org/fcrepo/http/commons/exceptionhandlers/MalformedRdfExceptionMapper.java#L39
Do you think the base64 encoded exception message is any more "machine-readable" than a link to a URL of a static web page detailing the constraint?

Also, have you verified that all of the POST/PATCH scenarios that result in triples not being persisted are resulting in a thrown MalformedRdfException? I was under the impression that some cases are still failing silently.

Because the link encoded data is the same as the response body then what ever you see is what the client machine would decode. So I think that could be more usable than a static webpage that says "We don't accept POST/PATCH requests for subjects not in domain." The current way we can provide the actual data, which can then be dealt with or sent back to the end user.

The alternative would require an additional field in the exception to specify which constraint has been violated. This would also require maintaining a list and associated webpages for each of these constraints.

I'm not sure if there is a benefit of one way over the other. I just thought it might be nice and easy to send our exceptions in a machine parable format. I.e. one piece of data per line, with certain consistent headers for the exceptions.
I have not verified all post and patch implementations. I'll do some more tests this week and see if any are silent.
Ok, some more review has found that PUT and POST operations that contain out of domain subjects in the RDF body have those silently removed and the rest is processed.
This happens here:
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-kernel-impl/src/main/java/org/fcrepo/kernel/impl/utils/iterators/PersistingRdfStreamConsumer.java#L92
So I'm removing
's
entire predicate filter
Instead I just throw a MalformedRdfException in the operateOnTriples function right between these
two statements
This will probably be slightly slower than before, but there doesn't seem to be a way to
throw an exception from inside the Guava predicate filter
. So we have to check each statement to see if we fail.
I'll have a pull request to present shortly and if there is a better suggestion I am more than happy to hear it.
No,
, there is no way to throw a
checked
exception from within a Guava Predicate, or for that matter, a Java 8 Predicate. You can and should throw an appropriate unchecked exception from within that Predicate.

2) Generate a JSON exception message body. For example:

4.2.1.6 LDP servers must publish any constraints on LDP clients’ ability to create or update LDPRs, by adding a Link header with an appropriate context URI, a link relation of
http://www.w3.org/ns/ldp#constrainedBy,

and a target URI identifying a set of constraints [RFC5988], to all responses to requests that fail due to violation of those constraints. For example, a server that refuses resource creation requests via HTTP PUT, POST, or PATCH would return this Link header on its 4xx responses to such requests. The same Link header may be provided on other responses. LDP neither defines nor constrains the representation of the link's target resource. Natural language constraint documents are therefore permitted, although machine-readable ones facilitate better client interactions. The appropriate context URI can vary based on the request's semantics and method; unless the response is otherwise constrained, the default (the effective request URI) should be used.

renderedFields.description: 4.2.1.6 LDP servers must publish any constraints on LDP clients’ ability to create or update LDPRs, by adding a Link header with an appropriate context URI, a link relation of http://www.w3.org/ns/ldp#constrainedBy, and a target URI identifying a set of constraints [RFC5988], to all responses to requests that fail due to violation of those constraints. For example, a server that refuses resource creation requests via HTTP PUT, POST, or PATCH would return this Link header on its 4xx responses to such requests. The same Link header may be provided on other responses. LDP neither defines nor constrains the representation of the link's target resource. Natural language constraint documents are therefore permitted, although machine-readable ones facilitate better client interactions. The appropriate context URI can vary based on the request's semantics and method; unless the response is otherwise constrained, the default (the effective request URI) should be used.
